title: Medicaid and CHIP coverage for pregnancy and postpartum, by state
methodology: Income limits are KFF and Georgetown CCF's 50-state survey figures as of January 2026 (KFF State Health Facts and Table 2 of the April 2026 report). They are percentages of the federal poverty level (FPL), converted to MAGI standards, and include the standard 5-percentage-point income disregard at the highest Medicaid level when the state does not cover pregnancy through CHIP. chipLimitFplPct is CHIP coverage of pregnant individuals (7 states); unbornChildLimitFplPct is CHIP's From Conception to End of Pregnancy (formerly unborn child) option (25 states); highestLimitFplPct is the highest of the three, which KFF calls the upper income limit. Postpartum status is KFF's Medicaid Postpartum Coverage Extension Tracker as of July 15, 2026. postpartumExtensionEffective is the effective date in each state's CMS approval letter (state plan amendment or section 1115 waiver), read from the documents KFF links, or the state's own announcement where noted; some states covered postpartum people for 12 months earlier with state funds or an earlier waiver (KFF). Presumptive eligibility reflects KFF/CCF's January 2025 survey (the January 2026 report does not cover it) for the Medicaid pregnancy group, updated where a state source shows a later change; it is left blank where the state did not report or we could not confirm a change. Hospitals in every state may make presumptive eligibility determinations, even in states that do not otherwise use it. Program names, agencies and application pages were checked on each state's site on 2026-10-09; Kansas, Mississippi and New Hampshire block automated checks, so their links come from the state listings on Medicaid.gov. Poverty guidelines are the 2026 HHS figures from the Federal Register. Each state's one-sentence answer is generated from these figures. Its dollar amount applies the highest income limit to the 2026 HHS guideline for a household of two (a pregnant person expecting one baby counts as two under 42 CFR 435.603), using the Alaska or Hawaii guideline where applicable. States apply their own rounding and update dates, so treat it as approximate.

povertyGuidelines2026.note: Annual income in dollars. Medicaid and CHIP limits are percentages of these figures; most programs update to new guidelines early each year.

federalFloorFplPct.text: States must cover pregnancy for individuals with income up to 138% FPL; most states (38) set the upper limit at or above 200% FPL. The median upper limit is 213% FPL (January 2026).

householdSizeRule.text: For Medicaid, a pregnant woman's family size counts her plus the number of children she is expected to deliver (42 CFR 435.603(b)).

postpartum12Month.text: Federal law requires pregnancy-related Medicaid through 60 days postpartum. The American Rescue Plan Act of 2021 gave states the option to extend it to 12 months starting April 1, 2022, and the Consolidated Appropriations Act, 2023 made the option permanent. As of July 15, 2026, 49 states and DC have implemented 12 months (Wisconsin started July 1, 2026); Arkansas is the only state still at 60 days.

workRequirementsExemption.text: Public Law 119-21 (2025) requires states to apply Medicaid work (community engagement) requirements to expansion adults ages 19-64 starting no later than January 1, 2027 (states may start earlier; HHS may grant good-faith exemptions that end by December 31, 2028). People who are pregnant or entitled to postpartum coverage are exempt, as are parents and caretakers of a dependent child 13 or younger.

presumptiveEligibility.text: Presumptive eligibility lets qualified providers such as clinics and hospitals enroll a pregnant person in temporary Medicaid right away while the full application is processed. In January 2025, 28 states used it for pregnant people in Medicaid. Hospitals in every state may make presumptive eligibility determinations if they choose to. Alabama added it on October 1, 2025.

immigrantEligibilityChange.text: Beginning October 1, 2026, federal Medicaid and CHIP funding for non-emergency care is generally limited to U.S. citizens and nationals, lawful permanent residents, Cuban/Haitian entrants and COFA migrants. States that elected the CHIPRA 214 option may still cover lawfully residing children and pregnant women without the 5-year wait. Emergency Medicaid is not affected.

AK.summary: In Alaska, Alaska Medicaid (Denali KidCare) covers pregnancy for household incomes up to 230% of the federal poverty level (about $62,215 a year for a household of two); Medicaid postpartum coverage lasts 12 months.
AK.agencyName: Alaska Department of Health, Division of Public Assistance

AL.summary: In Alabama, Alabama Medicaid covers pregnancy for household incomes up to 146% of the federal poverty level and CHIP up to 317% (about $68,599 a year for a household of two); Medicaid postpartum coverage lasts 12 months.
AL.notes: Between 146% and 317% FPL, coverage is through CHIP's From Conception to End of Pregnancy option, which covers the pregnancy (the unborn child) regardless of the parent's immigration status; benefits and postpartum coverage under this option can be narrower than full Medicaid. Alabama started Presumptive Eligibility for Pregnancy (PEP) on October 1, 2025 (Act 2025-204), after KFF's January 2025 survey.
